title: What philosophy is
description: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about reality, knowledge and value, and answers them mainly by building and examining arguments.

facts.text: Philosophy asks deep, fundamental questions about the nature of the universe and ourselves, the limits of human knowledge and values, such as whether a law is fair; a physicist asks what caused an event, a philosopher whether causation exists at all.

Philosophical questions can’t be settled by purely empirical means: no lab experiment can test whether a society should value equality over freedom, though philosophers often use scientific findings as premises.
The main method of philosophy is to build and examine arguments: reasons, called premises, offered to support a conclusion.
When a question becomes open to rigorous experiment it tends to leave philosophy for its own field: the natural sciences were once called natural philosophy.
Most doctoral degrees are called Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), even in subjects such as chemistry.
Thales in Greece (about 620-546 BCE), Confucius in China (traditionally 551-479 BCE) and the Buddha in India (flourished about 450 BCE) lived within a few centuries of one another.

title: The branches of philosophy
description: Philosophy’s main branches each ask one kind of question: metaphysics (what exists), epistemology (what we can know), ethics (how to act and live), logic (good reasoning), aesthetics (beauty and art) and political philosophy (society and justice).

facts.text: Metaphysics studies what sorts of things exist, what the world is made of, and how things cause or explain each other.
Epistemology, from the Greek episteme (knowledge), studies knowledge, evidence and justified belief, such as whether we can trust our senses.
Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks what makes actions right or wrong and what makes a person or a life good.
Logic studies good and bad arguments and reasoning.
Aesthetics is the theory of beauty and, more broadly, the philosophy of art.
Political philosophy begins with the question of what a person’s relationship to society ought to be, and asks what makes a society just or unjust.

The word metaphysics comes from Ta meta ta phusika, ’the ones after the physical ones’, a title an editor, probably Andronicus of Rhodes, gave Aristotle’s books at least a century after his death; Aristotle never knew the word.

title: Thought experiments
description: A thought experiment tests an idea by imagining a carefully built case instead of running a real one, as in Galileo’s tied balls or Glaucon’s ring of Gyges; critics such as Kathleen Wilkes doubt how much they prove.

facts.text: Thought experiments are devices of the imagination: instead of running a real experiment, you imagine a scenario and reason about it; they are used in philosophy, physics, mathematics, economics and other fields.

Galileo imagined tying a heavy ball to a light one: on Aristotle’s view that heavier bodies fall faster, the pair would fall both slower (the light one holds back the heavy) and faster (together they are heavier), a contradiction.
In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of the shepherd Gyges, who finds a ring that makes him invisible and uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the kingdom.
Glaucon imagines giving one ring to a just person and one to an unjust person, and argues both would act alike, because people are just only when they cannot safely be unjust.
Kathleen Wilkes argued in Real People (1988) that thought experiments, especially about personal identity, give inconclusive and unconvincing results, and preferred real cases.

title: Plato’s Forms
description: Plato held that perfect, eternal, unchanging Forms such as Beauty, Equality or Circle, known by thought rather than the senses, are more real than the changing things we see; his own Parmenides raises the Third Man objection.

facts.text: Plato held that beyond the world our senses show us is a more real and perfect realm of Forms, such as Beauty, Justice and Equality, which are eternal and changeless.
Plato’s most basic distinction is between the many things that appear beautiful and the one Form that is what beauty really is; things are beautiful by sharing in, or participating in, that Form.
On a standard reading of Plato, the Form Circle is perfectly circular, while every drawn circle or round ball falls short of it.
For Plato the Forms are grasped by thought, not by the senses: they exist in a realm available only to thought.

In Plato’s Phaedo, Socrates argues that equal sticks and stones sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal, while Equality itself never appears unequal, so our knowledge of Equality cannot have come from the sticks.

In Plato’s dialogue Parmenides, the Third Man argument (named by Aristotle) objects that if large things share the Form Large and that Form is itself large, a further Form is needed, and so on forever; scholars disagree whether Plato thought it fatal.

title: Aristotle’s four causes
description: Aristotle explained anything, such as a bronze statue, by four causes: material (what it is made of), formal (what it is), efficient (where the change came from) and final (what it is for); he placed form inside things, and Bacon later wanted final causes out of physics.

facts.text: Aristotle held that we know a thing only when we grasp its cause, its ’why’; his four causes are four kinds of answer to a why-question, and a full explanation can call on all four.
The material cause answers ’What is it made out of?’: for a bronze statue, the bronze.
The formal cause answers ’What is it?’: its form or essence; for a bronze statue, the shape the melted bronze is poured into.
The efficient cause answers ’Where does the change come from?’: for a bronze statue, Aristotle points most precisely to the art of bronze-casting in the sculptor.
The final cause is that for the sake of which something is done: the model, the mold and the melting and pouring of bronze are all for the sake of the finished statue.
Aristotle, who studied at Plato’s Academy, rejected Plato’s separately existing Forms: for him form exists in the thing, so a bronze sphere’s bronze and roundness are not two separate things.

In The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon argued that final causes, such as clouds being ’for’ watering the earth, belong to metaphysics, and that mixing them into physics had held back the search for physical causes.

title: Confucius and the junzi
description: Confucius turned the junzi from a person of noble birth into a person of moral nobility, marked by ren (humaneness) expressed through li (ritual propriety) performed with real feeling; the Mohists attacked costly Confucian rituals.

facts.text: Confucius (traditionally 551-479 BCE) is known mainly through the Analects, an early text of his sayings and conversations with disciples.
The word junzi originally meant ’prince’s son’; Confucius was a pivotal figure in turning it from a person of noble blood into a person of moral nobility who could come from any background.
Early English translations rendered junzi as ’gentleman’; Ames and Rosemont suggested ’exemplary person’.
Ren, the broadest Confucian virtue, is translated benevolence, humaneness or goodness; the Analects defines it as ’caring for others’ (12.22).
Before Confucius, ren referred to the aristocracy of bloodlines, something like the strong and handsome look of an aristocrat; in the Analects it is a moral excellence anyone can achieve.
Li, ritual propriety, covers the conventions of ritual and etiquette, down to what to wear; asked about ren, Confucius spoke of overcoming oneself and returning to ritual propriety (12.1).
Confucius said he could not bear ritual without reverence or mourning without grief, and that at funerals the mourners’ distress matters more than the formalities.

The Mohists, followers of Mozi, argued that lavish funerals and lengthy mourning, customs the Confucians promoted, bring poverty, a smaller population and disorder, so are not what a benevolent person would do.

title: The Dao and wu wei
description: The Daodejing, credited to Laozi, teaches the Dao (the Way) and wu wei, acting without forcing, modelled on water; Zhuangzi’s Butcher Ding shows it in practice, and Confucians such as Xunzi pushed back.

facts.text: Laozi, the ’Old Master’, is said by Chinese sources to have lived in the 6th century BCE and to have written the Daodejing, but some modern scholars think he is entirely legendary.
Dao means ’way’: the Chinese graph suggests a path, and the word came to mean the right course.
The Daodejing opens, in James Legge’s translation: ’The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.’
Wu wei, often translated ’non-action’ or ’effortless action’, does not mean total inaction; in the Daodejing it contrasts with action driven by self-serving desire.

The Daodejing compares the highest excellence to water, which benefits all things without striving and takes the low place people dislike, and says nothing is softer than water yet nothing beats it at attacking the hard and strong.

In the Zhuangzi, Butcher Ding carves oxen by steering his blade through the natural gaps between the joints, so his knife is still sharp after 19 years, while a good cook changes knives every year and a mediocre one every month.
Zhuangzi, a later Daoist philosopher, lived in the 300s BCE; the IEP dates him about 369-298 BCE.
The Daodejing (ch. 38) says ritual propriety appears only after the Dao is lost, calling it a thin form of loyalty and good faith and the beginning of disorder.
The Confucian Xunzi criticized Zhuangzi as valuing nature so highly that he failed to see the value of the human.

title: The no-self argument
description: Buddhist philosophers argued that a person is a name for five changing aggregates with no lasting self behind them, as Nagasena showed King Milinda with the chariot; Nyaya critics replied that memory needs an enduring self.

facts.text: The Buddha’s teaching of non-self (anatman) denies that any of the elements making up a person is a self, and classical Indian philosophers understood him to deny the self altogether.
Buddhist thought treats a person as five kinds of aggregates (skandhas): body, feelings, perceptions, volitions and consciousness.
Buddhist philosophers held that all these elements are impermanent, so none of them can be the lasting self.
The Questions of King Milinda records a dialogue between the Buddhist monk Nagasena and King Milinda, usually identified with the Indo-Greek king Menander I (about 150 BCE).
Nagasena tells the king that ’Nagasena’ is only a designation in common use, with no permanent self behind it; the king retorts that then Nagasena is a mere empty sound and he has spoken a falsehood.

Nagasena asks whether the chariot is the pole, the axle, the wheels or other parts, all of them together, or something outside them; the king says no each time, then agrees ’chariot’ is a name used on account of the parts.
Buddhist philosophers call a chariot conventionally real: a convenient single name for its parts assembled the right way, not something over and above them; a person is the same.

Nyaya philosophers Vatsyayana and Uddyotakara objected that if I were a different self from yesterday’s ’me’, I could not remember what that ’me’ experienced; Buddhists replied that causal links within one stream of events are enough.

title: India’s schools of philosophy
description: Classical Indian schools gave rival answers: Nyaya’s logic of inference (smoke and fire), Advaita Vedanta’s identity of self and Brahman, Carvaka materialism trusting perception alone, and the Jain view that truth is many-sided.

facts.text: The oldest surviving Nyaya text is the Nyaya-sutra attributed to Gautama (about 200 CE).
Nyaya accepts four means of knowledge (pramanas): perception, inference, comparison and testimony.
Nyaya’s model inference: the hill has fire, because it has smoke, and wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen hearth and unlike a lake.

Advaita (’non-dual’) Vedanta, promoted by Shankara, who probably lived in the 8th century, holds that Brahman is the fundamental reality under everything and that the individual self is in reality identical with it, its separateness an illusion.
The Carvaka (Lokayata) materialists accepted perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge, rejecting testimony and inferences about what cannot be experienced.
The Carvakas held that consciousness is a product of the material body.

Jain philosophers hold that reality is many-sided (anekanta), so no single view captures the whole truth, an idea illustrated by the story of blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it differently.

title: Greek, Chinese and Indian beginnings
description: Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live in different ways: Plato and Aristotle on Forms and form, Chinese thinkers on how to live and govern, Indian schools on the self.

facts.text: Early Chinese philosophy addressed rulers as well as individuals: training in li was part of preparing rulers and officials, and the Daodejing says that when the sage governs through non-action, good order is universal (ch. 3).
Classical Indian schools disagreed sharply about the self: Buddhist philosophers denied a lasting self, Nyaya defended an enduring self, and Advaita Vedanta identified the self with Brahman.
